en: Trail he could follow without going astray.
Even when going alone, that wondrous one,
Wolf Bakai, the leopard—
He was the hawk; he was the support.
Making people grasp what they had not grasped,
That was the hero Bakai, the hawk.
“Of Sultan Manas, the leopard,
I had known that he was a lion.
From God Most High, the One,
‘Grant me Manas!’
That is what I kept asking.
You have chosen to lodge your guest,
Chosen to have him tell his tale,
Chosen to have him draw his line.
My magnanimous one, met along the way,
You have chosen to hear the wonders.
You have chosen to draw from within me
The festering, pain-filled turmoil.
Let me sing; listen to my song.
I shall tell my secret as faithfully as my creed.
My friend, listen to my words;
Know that what I tell is true.
My lion Manas, heed my words.
Its base and its stock,
Cast of lamb-liver steel—
Its like could not be found.
That peerless iron, Almabash,
Makes no distinction between far and near.
It would not fail for sixty days;
When they heated and forged it,
They twisted six grooves into it.
No man could find another like it;
The foes it met lay fallen.
When slung upon the body, that wondrous thing
Was a mirror upon the shoulder blades.
When turned against contending foes,
It was the solace of a life held in trust.
My blood-drinker, that you would be born
And come forth, I had known.
For the noble, fierce-maned one to take,
To bring slaughter upon the world—
My magnanimous one, for you yourself
I had been fitting it.
Its stock was cast and skillfully worked;
The Black Smith, David's friend,
That poor fellow made it.
Having its stock fashioned from tempered steel,
As the price for that wretched thing,
I had exactly a thousand young mares given.
I had the steel drawn slender,
Had it fired to split a target,
Had skilled hands fit it together,
Had mighty experts test it.
That formidable Akkelte—
I had its sight set with a jewel,
A sight that satisfied the heart.
Gold and silver together
I had fastened upon its side.
I had it wrapped in precious cloth
And kept where people would not see it.
If we find it, that is the treasure;
It will meet a fortunate hero,
That tempered steel whose like cannot be found.
A living gun, that wondrous thing:
When it sees the massed enemy,
Blood flows from its ears;
It cracks and fires of itself.
When the enemy draws near,
Its bullets flash as they fly forth;
Its voice bellows like a camel calf.
Its bullet striking squarely—
No enemy can withstand it.
Where it strikes is flame, a blazing fire;
No man can stand and face it.
If the fired bullet strikes straight on,
Not a handspan of bone can be found.
That peerless gun Akkelte—
I knew that it was alive.
For my fierce-maned Manas to take,
I had dedicated it to you!
Writing words in Arabic,
I placed an inscription in its middle;
I gave it the name Akkelte.
If my champion came into my hands,
For my impetuous Manas to take it,
Upon the enemy who came to face him
To heap distress and tribulation,
Of Beijing, untouched by Chaliyar,
For my fierce-maned one's strength to suffice
To seize its khanship—
I had been fitting it for this.
I had it wrapped in silk
And covered with leather.
Back then, riding my gray steed,
Unable to find you, my fierce-maned one,
When I was grieving greatly,
Back then, turning my gray steed's head,
With fire burning through my very innards,
When I could no longer bear it,
Where my cord was cut and my birth-clothes washed,
Where birth-blood fell, I had no land.
To know how I was faring,
I had no dear Kyrgyz people.
Sleeping, in my dream,
I saw Manas indistinctly.
‘Where shall I find him?’
I kept wandering in sorrow.
A fortress-house set across the way—
When my hawk came to mind,
My wretched life seemed less than a handspan.
Somehow to find Manas,
To attain my wish—
If I could not find Manas,
From this deceitful world
To depart in sacrificial death—
Without sparing my wretched life,
I rode far and wide.
What ears had heard of and eyes had seen—
I wandered through every land.
I brought hardship upon their game.
For six months, seven months, I myself
Went away on a long hunt.
Frenzied, chasing wild asses,
Crossing hills and rough ridges,
Treading many kinds of land,
Without a cloud the size of a knucklebone breaking away,
Without the mountain's edge appearing,
Beyond the reach of the eye,
The towering snowy mountains—
Where they led could not be known.
Finding no hollow the size of a saddlecloth,
Finding no hill the size of a knucklebone,
Pursuing wild asses, drawing close,
I wandered lost for six months.
By a pine growing on the plain,
I slaughtered a mare with a foal.
Not a crow gave a caw;
Not a raven gave a croak.
‘This land is deserted,’ I thought.
The sacred Akkelte
I put away in a hidden store.
When two years had passed,
Counting them in months,
When twenty-four months had passed,
As the people moved up to the highlands,
In the season when grazing blackens horses' tongues,
When the poppy grass turned red,
When the earth was full of flowers,
The dappled roans gleamed with fat,
The wild asses rolled and grew sleek,
Men and beasts were running wild,
When horses' tongues grew dark with grass,
When yellow floodwater rose and overflowed,
Greening the surface of the earth,
When a carpet of light spread over it,
Streams ran and flowers filled the land,
To see what he had left in safekeeping
The day came for your Bakay to think.
Running wild in pursuit of wild asses,
I had scoured the barren plain.
Then it came into my mind;
That treasure I had left in trust,
I went, saying, ‘Let me see it.’
Traveling tirelessly for three months,
Going far, not sparing my horse,
To look upon my treasure,
When I came to the pine,
Sixty men, surveyors of the land,
Had come there from afar.
Within the pine
They had discovered that cache.
They had scattered my markers and gone,
They had long since brought me ruin.
They had opened all my markings,
They had scattered my stored belongings.
They had brought me hardship now;
‘It is an irreplaceable treasure,’ they said,
And put it in their treasury;
The matchless gun Akkelte,
They had locked it safely away.
I followed their tracks,
I gave my gray steed its head.
Relentlessly pursuing their trail,
I followed them until I wasted away.
Tracking them by day and night,
I entered their city.
‘Agree to what I say,’ I said,
‘Give me Akkelte,’ I said,
And sent word to them.
A curse upon being alone!
I have no support to rely upon,
I have no stronghold where I dwell.
To confront them in battle,
To seize Akkelte back,
My champion, I have no hero like you.
I have no cliff a goose cannot circle,
I have no mountain to shelter behind.
If I fought fiercely for six months,
I have no fresh swift horse to ride.
To stand beside me as my support,
I have no strong kinsman like you.
When I think, ‘Let me attack,’
The dark house, its side crumbling,
My wretched soul is less than a handful.
Rousing myself, beseeching God,
To find you,
Because of Akkelte,
That is where my thoughts dwell.
Of costly, excellent workmanship,
When he thinks of Akkelte,
Bakay cannot bear to stand still.
Because of what has happened,
Because of Akkelte,
I fell ill once for six months.
Unless I seize Akkelte back,
When will my burning grief subside?
The living gun Akkelte,
Taken hunting, it brings delight;
Taken to war, it brings destruction.
My insides are black, my liver an ember;
Your Bakay has no regret.
That Kelte is an inheritance,
I, grieving Bakay, know.
‘If my Manas comes,
Let me seize Kelte back,’ I say,
And have been praying for that.
If you heed my words, my wolf-maned one,
Let us go near their settlement.
Even if we are massacred now,
Let us seize Akkelte back.
Let us send an envoy to their people,
Let us surround their settlement.
If they will not heed our words,
If they will not give Akkelte,
Let us find a way.
Striking after nightfall, not by day,
Let us storm their palace one night,
Let us scatter their plentiful herds.
‘Give us Akkelte!’ let us say.
If they will not give Akkelte,
If they will not heed our words,
Let us take our booty and return.
From now on, out on the plain,
Let us make them fear to roam.
Other caches they encounter,
Let us make them fear to touch.
Let us not stand watching here;
Let us not rest without Akkelte.
Driving them off and following behind,
For the pain Akkelte has caused,
Let us scatter their four kinds of livestock.
Let us raid their mares,
And if their owner draws near,
Let us pound his brains and lay him low,
Let us teach him a lesson.
Let us bind him fast,
